linear ODEs . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 78 2 1 Lecture 1 1.1 Vector spaces Let F be a field. Informally, a field is a set of numbers equipped with the operations +, −, ×, ÷ that satisfy the usual arithmetic rules. A precise mathematical definition is not required in this course; for a rigorous treatment and an introduction to the beautiful Galois theory of fields, see [1, Chapters 13-14]. In this course, we will primarily focus on the cases where F = R, the field of real numbers, or F = C, the field of complex numbers. What is a vector? Mathematicians do not answer the question directly. Instead we answer the question what operations can be done on vectors. As long as these operations can be done, they are vectors. Definition 1.1. A set V is called a vector space (linear space) over F if it is equipped with addition V × V → V, (x, y) ↦→ x + y and scalar multiplication F × V → V, (a, x) ↦→ ax satisfying the following axioms: for any a, b ∈ F , x, y, z ∈ V (I) x + y = y + x, commutativity (II) (x + y) + z = x + (y + z), associativity (III) There exists 0 ∈ V such that x + 0 = x, additive identity (IV) For any x ∈ V , there exists −x ∈ V such that x + (−x) = 0, additive inverse (V) a(bx) = (ab)x, multiplicative associativity (VI) 1x = x, multiplicative identity (VII) a(x + y) = ax + ay, distributive property 1 (VIII) (a + b)x = ax + bx. distributive property 2 An element x ∈ V is called a vector and an element a ∈ F is called a scalar. Remark 1.2. The axioms above seems a lot, but they are just saying that the usual algebraic rules work for vector addition and scalar multiplication. This can be seen even more clearly in Proposition 1.3. It should be noted that the multiplication of two vectors is not defined within the structure of a vector space. Proposition 1.3. The following are direct consequences of the axioms (i) The element 0 ∈ V is unique. 3 (ii) For any x ∈ V , 0x = 0. (iii) For any a ∈ F , a0 = 0. (iv) If a ∈ F , x ∈ V such that ax = 0, then either a = 0 (in F ) or x = 0 (in V ). (v) For any x ∈ V , the element −x is unique. (vi) For any x ∈ V , (−1)x = −x. (vii) If x + z = y + z, then x = y. Proof. (i)-(vi) are left as exercise. We now proof (vii). We have x = x + 0 = x + (z + (−z)) = (x + z) + (−z) = (y + z) + (−z) = y + (z + (−z)) = y + 0 = y where we used (III), (IV), (II), the assumption, (II), (IV), (III) in each equality. Example 1.4. A subset W ⊂ V of a vector space V is called a subspace if (i) 0 ∈ W (ii) For any x, y ∈ W , we have x + y ∈ W (iii) For any a ∈ F , x ∈ W , we have ax ∈ W Lemma 1.9. A subspace is a vector space. Proof. We first show that if x ∈ W then −x ∈ W . By Proposition 1.3 (v) and definition of a subspace, −x = (−1)x ∈ W . By the definition of a subspace, addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined on W . The axioms (I)-(VIII) are satisfied on W since they are satisfied for any vectors in V . Example 1.10. A line through the origin in R3 is given by {tv : t ∈ R} where v = (v1, v2, v3)t ̸= 0 is the direction of the line. A plane through the origin in R3 is given by {tv + sw : t, s ∈ R} where v, w are two vectors in R3 not parallel to each other. One can check that lines and planes are subspaces of R3. In fact {0}, lines, planes, R3 are the only subspaces of R3. Example 1.11. A matrix A is called a square matrix if the number of columns is the same as the number of rows i.e. A ∈ Mn×n(F ). A square matrix is symmetric if A = At. It is anti-symmetric if At = −A. The set of symmetric matrices and anti- symmetric matrices are subspaces of Mn×n(F ) can be seen as follows: 0 matrix is both symmetric and anti-symmetric and for any A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ) we have (A + B)t = At + Bt and (cA)t = cAt. Thus if A, B are symmetric, then (A + B)t = At + Bt = A + B and (cA)t = cAt = cA. The anti-symmetric case is similar. Example 1.12. Ck(R) is a subspace of Ck−1(R) for any k ∈ N. Pn(R) is a subspace of Ck(R) for any k ∈ N. Solutions to a linear differential equation form a subspace. Example 1.13. Let V = {f ∈ C2(R) : f ′′ + f = 0} with the addition and scalar multiplication from C2(R). Then V is a subspace of C2(R) since 0 ∈ V and if f, g ∈ V and c ∈ R, we have (f + g)′′ + f + g = 0 and (cf )′′ + cf = 0. In fact, we know from ODE that f (x) = c1 cos x + c2 sin x for c1, c2 ∈ R from which one can also check that V is a subspace. The point here is that we do not need the explicit formula for solutions to conclude that the set of all solutions form a subspace. 6 1.3 Span We want to build the vector space out of the smallest amount of vectors. Addition and scalar multiplication are the only operations we have in a vector space. If we have x, y ∈ V , then x + y and ax for a ∈ F can be built out of them. Given a set of vectors v1, . . . , vn what are all vectors that can be built from them? This is the idea of linear combination and span. Definition 1.14. Let V be a vector space over F . A linear combination of v1, . . . , vn ∈ V is a vector of the form a1v1 + · · · + anvn where a1, . . . , an ∈ F . The set of all linear combinations of v1, . . . , vn is denoted by span(v1, . . . , vn). We use the convention that span ∅ = {0}. Proposition 1.15. span(v1, . . . , vn) is a subspace of V . Proof. By Proposition 1.3 (ii), we have 0 = 0v1 + · · · + 0vn ∈ span(v1, . . . , vn). If x = a1v1 + · · · + anvn and y = b1v1 + · · · + bnvn are two linear combinations, then x + y = (a1 + b1)v1 + · · · + (an + bn)vn and cx = (ca1)v1 + · · · + (can)vn are both linear combinations of v1, . . . , vn. Thus span(v1, . . . , vn) is a subspace. Example 1.16. Let v1 = (1, 0, 0)t. Then span(v1) = {(a1, 0, 0)t : a1 ∈ R} is the line through the origin in the direction of v1. Let v2 = (0, 1, 0)t, then span(v1, v2) = {(a1, a2, 0)t : a1, a2 ∈ R} is the plane deter- mined by 0, v and v2. Let v3 = (1, 1, 0)t, then span(v1, v2, v3) = {(a1 + a3, a2 + a3, 0)t : a1, a2, a3 ∈ R}. This is the same as span(v1, v2) since it is just the set of points with x3 = 0. Let v4 = (0, 0, 1)t, then span(v1, v2, x) = {(a1, a2, a3)t : a1, a2, a3 ∈ R} = R3. Definition 1.17. v1, . . . , vn is a spanning set of V if span(v1, . . . , vn) = V . If V has a finite spanning set, then V is called a finite dimensional vector space. 1.4 Linear dependence and independence We see in Example 2.3 that v3 is redundant in building vectors i.e. adding v3 to v1, v2 does not change their span. We want to get rid of the redundant vectors to find the smallest set of vectors that span a vector space. The following concepts are important. Definition 1.18. v1, . . . , vn is linearly dependent if there exist a1, . . . , an ∈ F not all zero such that a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0. v1, . . . , vn is linearly independent if or it is not linearly dependent, in other words, for any a1, . . . , an ∈ F such that a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0 we have a1 = · · · = an = 0. Example 1.19. v1 = (1, 0, 0)t, v2 = (0, 1, 0)t are linearly independent since for any a1, a2 ∈ F we have 0 = a1v1 + a2v2 = (a1, a2, 0)t implies a1 = a2 = 0. 7 Example 1.20. v1 = (1, 0, 0)t, v2 = (0, 1, 0)t, v3 = (1, 1, 0)t are linearly dependent since v1 + v2 − v3 = 0. The previous examples shows that a linearly dependent set of vectors is not small enough i.e. it has vectors that is redundant and that linearly independent vectors are not redundant. Thus our goal of finding a smallest set of vectors that builds the whole vector space is to find a basis: Definition 1.21. v1, . . . , vn is a basis of V if span(v1, . . . , vn) = V and v1, . . . , vn are linearly independent. (i) v1, . . . , vn is linearly dependent if and only if there exists 1 ≤ k ≤ n such that vk ∈ span(v1, . . . , vk−1). (ii) v1, . . . , vn is linearly independent if and only if for any 1 ≤ k ≤ n we have vk /∈ span(v1, . . . , vk−1). Remark 2.9. If k = 1, we use the convention that (v1, . . . , vk−1) is the empty set and span ∅ = {0}. Proof. Note that statement (ii) is logically the negation of statement (i), we only need to show (i). “=⇒” Since v1, . . . , vn is linearly dependent, there exist a1, . . . , an ∈ F not all zero such that a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0. Let k be the largest index such that ak ̸= 0. Then we have a1v1 + · · · + akvk = 0. Thus if k > 1, then vk = − 1 ak (a1v1 + · · · + ak−1vk−1). If k = 1, then a1v1 = 0 and hence v1 = 0 by Proposition 1.3 (iv). “⇐=” If vk ∈ span(v1, . . . , vk−1), then there exists a1, . . . , ak−1 ∈ F such that vk = a1v1 + · · · + ak−1vk−1. In other words, a1v1 + · · · + ak−1vk−1 − vk = 0. This shows v1, . . . , vn are linearly dependent. 2.3 Basis The previous examples shows that a linearly dependent set of vectors is not small enough i.e. it has vectors that are redundant. On the other hand, linearly independent vectors are not redundant. Thus our goal of finding a smallest set of vectors that builds the whole vector space is to find a basis: Definition 2.10. v1, . . . , vn is a basis of V if span(v1, . . . , vn) = V and v1, . . . , vn are linearly independent. We can reduce a spanning set to a basis by removing the “redundant” vectors as in the following lemma. Lemma 2.11. Every spanning set contains a basis. Proof. Let v1, . . . , vn be a spanning set i.e. span(v1, . . . , vn) = V . We remove vectors in v1, . . . , vn through the following process. Step 1: if v1 = 0, then delete v1. If v1 ̸= 0, leave it unchanged. Step k: if vk ∈ span(v1, . . . , vk−1) then delete vk. Otherwise leave vk unchanged. 10 Stop the process after step n. We relabel the remaining vectors as v1, . . . , vm pre- serving the original order. Since each time we discard a vector that is already in the span of previous vectors, we have span(v1, . . . , vm) = V . By construction we also have vk /∈ span(v1, . . . , vk−1) for any 1 ≤ k ≤ m. By Lemma 2.8, we have v1, . . . , vm is linearly independent. Thus v1, . . . , vm is a basis of V . We need the following Lemma for proving the main theorem of this lecture, Theorem 2.13. Lemma 2.12. Let v1, . . . , vn be a basis of V . If v1 = a1w1 + a2v2 + · · · + anvn where ai ∈ F , 1 ≤ i ≤ n and a1 ̸= 0, then w1, v2, . . . , vn is also a basis. Proof. Since v1 = a1w1 + a2v2 + · · · + anvn, we have x = x1(a1w1 + a2v2 + · · · + anvn) + x2v2 + · · · + xnvn = a1x1w + (a2x1 + x2)v2 + · · · + (anx1 + xn)vn. Thus span(w1, v2, . . . , vn) = V . Then since w1 = 1 a1 (v1 − a2v2 − · · · − anvn), we have b1 1 a1 (v1 − a2v2 − · · · − anvn) + b2v2 + · · · + bnvn = 0 i.e. b1 a1 v1 + (b2 − b1 a1 a2)v2 + · · · + (bn − b1 a1 an)vn = 0. Since v1, . . . , vn is a basis, we have b1 a1 = b2 − b1 a1 a2 = · · · = bn − b1 a1 an = 0. Hence b1 = · · · = bn = 0. Theorem 2.13 (Replacement theorem). Let v1, . . . , vn be a basis for V and w1, . . . , wm be linearly independent. Then reordering v1, . . . , vn if necessary, for each 1 ≤ k ≤ m, we have {w1, . . . , wk, vk+1, . . . , vn} is a basis of V . In particular n ≥ m. Proof. We prove the theorem inductively on k. We first prove that the conclusion is true for k = 1. Since v1, . . . , vn is a basis, w1 = a1v1 + · · · + anvn. Since w1, . . . , wm are linearly independent, w1 ̸= 0.
